title: SparkSession Initialization and Config
description: The entry point to programming Spark with the Dataset and DataFrame API. It explains how to build a local or cluster-connected Spark session with configurations optimized for cloud storage and adaptive query execution in Azure Databricks or Microsoft Fabric.
code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

# Build SparkSession with optimized configs for enterprise Medallion Pipelines
spark = SparkSession.builder \
    .appName("EU_BFSI_Transaction_Processor") \
    .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "200") \
    .config("spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled", "true") \
    .config("spark.databricks.delta.optimizeWrite.enabled", "true") \
    .config("spark.databricks.delta.autoCompact.enabled", "true") \
    .getOrCreate()

# Verify the active session details
print(f"Spark Version: {spark.version}")
print(f"Master Endpoint: {spark.sparkContext.master}")
print(f"App Name: {spark.sparkContext.appName}")
notes: Use SparkSession.builder to configure parameters before runtime.
CoalescePartitions avoids small file issues by shrinking partition counts after shuffle stages.
In Databricks and Microsoft Fabric, the SparkSession is pre-initialized as 'spark'.
OptimizeWrite and AutoCompact are Delta-specific properties essential for maintaining performance.
use_case: Initializing a PySpark pipeline for an EU BFSI data lakehouse in Azure Databricks, enabling baseline optimizations for Delta Lake writes.

title: Reading and Writing Delta Tables
description: Reading from and writing to Delta Lake tables, including standard write modes (append, overwrite) and format options. Delta Lake provides ACID transaction guarantees on top of cloud storage like ADLS Gen2 or Microsoft OneLake.
code:
# Read raw transaction data from Azure Data Lake Storage (ADLS) Gen2
bronze_df = spark.read.format("delta") \
    .load("abfss://bronze@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/ledger_logs")

# Filter only settled SEPA transfers for processing
sepa_txns_df = bronze_df.filter(
    (bronze_df.txn_type == "SEPA") & (bronze_df.status == "COMPLETED")
)

# Write to Silver layer with schema merging and overwrite mode
sepa_txns_df.write.format("delta") \
    .mode("overwrite") \
    .option("mergeSchema", "true") \
    .save("abfss://silver@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/sepa_transactions")
notes: Delta Lake uses transaction logs (.checkpoint files) to guarantee ACID properties.
overwrite mode replaces the entire directory atomically without causing downtime to readers.
mergeSchema allows schema evolution when new fields are introduced downstream.
Use abfss:// protocol for secure access to Azure storage accounts via OAuth or SAS tokens.
use_case: Ingesting raw payment logs from ADLS landing zone and promoting them to cleansed Silver tables in an Azure Databricks medallion environment.

title: DataFrame Schema Definition (StructType & StructField)
description: Programmatic definition of schemas to enforce type safety on ingestion, avoiding auto-schema inference performance costs and errors. This is critical when dealing with strictly structured files like regulatory bank exports.
code:
from pyspark.sql.types import StructType, StructField, StringType, DecimalType, TimestampType, DateType

# Enforce rigorous schema validation for incoming SWIFT payment files
swift_schema = StructType([
    StructField("swift_msg_id", StringType(), False),
    StructField("sender_bic", StringType(), False),
    StructField("receiver_bic", StringType(), False),
    StructField("txn_amount", DecimalType(18, 4), False),
    StructField("txn_currency", StringType(), False),
    StructField("value_date", DateType(), True),
    StructField("ingestion_ts", TimestampType(), True)
])

# Read incoming JSON files enforcing the strict schema
raw_swift_df = spark.read.format("json") \
    .schema(swift_schema) \
    .load("abfss://raw@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/swift_inbound/2026/*.json")
notes: Explicit schema definition prevents Spark from scanning the entire dataset to infer types, speeding up read operations.
DecimalType(18,4) is used for financial amounts to avoid floating-point representation errors.
Nullable flag (False/True) specifies if columns can accept null values during ingestion parsing.
Unmatched values in schema columns will be converted to NULL rather than failing the execution.
use_case: Enforcing static types on incoming SWIFT MT103 payment messages in Microsoft Fabric to guarantee data quality and audit compliance.

title: Basic Column Transformations (select, filter, withColumn, drop)
description: Fundamental transformations to project columns, filter records, add or modify columns, and remove unnecessary fields. These operations are evaluated lazily by Spark's Catalyst Optimizer.
code:
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, upper, round

# Load Silver transactions
silver_df = spark.read.format("delta").load("abfss://silver@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/transactions")

# Project relevant fields, apply currency conversion, and clean up raw columns
cleansed_df = silver_df.select("txn_id", "account_id", "txn_amount", "txn_currency", "fx_rate") \
    .filter(col("txn_amount") > 0) \
    .withColumn("txn_currency_clean", upper(col("txn_currency"))) \
    .withColumn("amount_eur", round(col("txn_amount") * col("fx_rate"), 2)) \
    .drop("txn_currency", "fx_rate")

# Show transformed schema
cleansed_df.printSchema()
notes: withColumn can overwrite an existing column if the names match, or create a new one.
Catalyst Optimizer merges multiple select() and filter() operations into a single execution step.
Using col('column_name') is preferred over df.column_name to avoid collisions with DataFrame methods.
Dropping source columns after transformation is a good practice to reduce memory usage during serialization.
use_case: Filtering out negative/null amounts and normalizing ISO currencies for retail banking transactions in the Silver layer.

title: Aggregations and GroupBy (groupBy, agg, sum, avg, count)
description: Grouping data by dimensions and performing aggregations like sum, count, and average. GroupBy operations trigger shuffles in a distributed system, reorganizing partitions based on the grouping keys.
code:
from pyspark.sql.functions import sum as _sum, avg, count, col

# Load transformed transaction data
df = spark.read.format("delta").load("abfss://silver@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/cleansed_transactions")

# Aggregate transactional volume and count by account for EBA reporting
monthly_summary_df = df.groupBy("account_id", "txn_currency_clean") \
    .agg(
        _sum("amount_eur").alias("total_volume_eur"),
        avg("amount_eur").alias("avg_txn_amount_eur"),
        count("txn_id").alias("txn_count")
    ) \
    .filter(col("total_volume_eur") > 100000)

# Display aggregate output
monthly_summary_df.show(10)
notes: Always import aggregate functions explicitly (e.g. from pyspark.sql.functions import sum as _sum) to avoid Python namespace collisions.
groupBy triggers a Wide Transformation (shuffle) where records are moved across network nodes.
Use agg() to apply multiple operations (sum, avg, count) simultaneously on the grouped dataset.
Add post-aggregation filters to limit the dataset size before writing to Gold tables.
use_case: Generating daily summary tables of transaction counts and volume by credit card holder for fraud detection thresholds.

title: Sorting and Deduplication (orderBy, sort, dropDuplicates)
description: Ordering data distributed across partitions and removing duplicate rows based on business keys. Clean and ordered data is critical for accurate reporting and optimized partition storage layouts.
code:
from pyspark.sql.functions import col

# Load duplicate-prone ledger stream
ledger_df = spark.read.format("delta").load("abfss://bronze@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/raw_ledger")

# Deduplicate based on transaction ID and audit timestamp
deduplicated_df = ledger_df.dropDuplicates(["txn_id", "txn_timestamp"])

# Sort within partitions to optimize write times and clustering performance
sorted_df = deduplicated_df.sortWithinPartitions("txn_date", "account_id")

# Global ordering (used strictly before small file output extracts)
ordered_report_df = sorted_df.orderBy(col("txn_timestamp").desc())
notes: dropDuplicates removes duplicate rows by keeping only the first occurrence for the specified business keys.
sortWithinPartitions is faster than sort() because it avoids a global shuffle across the network.
orderBy performs a global sort and collects data into sorted partitions, which can be computationally expensive.
Ensure you deduplicate early in the Silver layer to prevent cascading inconsistencies in reports.
use_case: Deduplicating incoming SEPA transactions in a multi-hop Medallion pipeline prior to running risk analytics.

title: Joining DataFrames (Inner, Left, Semi, Anti Joins)
description: Joining multiple DataFrames using various join types like inner, left, semi, and anti joins. Correct join selection is foundational to master dimensional enrichment and exception checking in Spark.
code:
# Load datasets
transactions = spark.read.format("delta").load("abfss://silver@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/transactions")
customer_profiles = spark.read.format("delta").load("abfss://silver@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/customers")
sanctioned_parties = spark.read.format("delta").load("abfss://silver@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/watchlist")

# 1. Left Join to enrich transactions with customer data
enriched_df = transactions.join(
    customer_profiles,
    on="customer_id",
    how="left"
)

# 2. Semi Join to extract transactions with matching sanctioned entities
flagged_txns_df = transactions.join(
    sanctioned_parties,
    transactions.counterparty_bic == sanctioned_parties.bic,
    how="left_semi"
)

# 3. Anti Join to isolate orphan records with no matching customer (Data Quality checks)
orphaned_df = transactions.join(
    customer_profiles,
    on="customer_id",
    how="left_anti"
)
notes: left_semi join returns columns strictly from the left DataFrame when there is a match, behaving like an IN subquery.
left_anti join returns rows from the left DataFrame when NO match is found, ideal for locating orphaned keys.
Specify join columns as strings (e.g. on='customer_id') to automatically deduplicate the key in the output schema.
Ensure join keys have matching data types to prevent implicit casting and slow execution plans.
use_case: Enriching customer records with risk scores, while filtering out invalid accounts and scanning for sanctioned counterparties.

title: Temporary Views & PySpark-SQL Interoperability
description: Creating session-scoped temporary views from DataFrames to enable query writing via Spark SQL. This enables seamless collaboration between Python data engineers and SQL business analysts.
code:
# Load Silver transactions DataFrame
silver_df = spark.read.format("delta").load("abfss://silver@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/transactions")

# Create temporary session-scoped view
silver_df.createOrReplaceTempView("v_silver_transactions")

# Execute standard ANSI SQL commands against the view
summary_report_df = spark.sql("""
    SELECT 
        account_id,
        SUM(txn_amount) as total_debited,
        CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() as report_generated_at
    FROM v_silver_transactions
    WHERE txn_type = 'DEBIT' AND status = 'COMPLETED'
    GROUP BY account_id
""")

# Show aggregate results
summary_report_df.show(5)
notes: Temporary views are bound to the active SparkSession and will be dropped when the session ends.
Global temporary views can be shared across multiple sessions using the 'global_temp.' prefix.
spark.sql() returns a PySpark DataFrame, allowing seamless chaining of Python and SQL expressions.
Always parameterize SQL queries to prevent formatting issues and query parsing failures.
use_case: Allowing SQL-native risk analysts to perform ad-hoc checks against a pre-cleansed PySpark DataFrame during regulatory audits.

title: Window Functions for Analytical Queries
description: Performing calculations across a set of rows related to the current row without collapsing them. Window functions are highly optimized by Spark for calculating running totals, rankings, and lagged records in financial workflows.
code:
from pyspark.sql import Window
from pyspark.sql.functions import row_number, col, lag, sum as _sum

# Define transaction window partition by account, ordered by timestamp
ranking_window = Window.partitionBy("account_id").orderBy(col("txn_timestamp").desc())
running_total_window = Window.partitionBy("account_id") \
    .orderBy("txn_timestamp") \
    .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)

# Enrich transactions with dynamic rankings and running balances
enriched_df = transactions \
    .withColumn("txn_recency", row_number().over(ranking_window)) \
    .withColumn("running_total_eur", _sum("amount_eur").over(running_total_window)) \
    .withColumn("prev_txn_amount", lag("amount_eur", 1, 0.0).over(ranking_window))

# Filter to get the top 3 most recent transactions per account
recent_txns_df = enriched_df.filter(col("txn_recency") <= 3)
notes: Window functions require partitioning and ordering to determine the partition boundaries and row sequence.
Use rowsBetween or rangeBetween to define sliding windows (e.g. running totals, moving averages).
lag and lead fetch rows at a specified offset relative to the current row, defaulting to a custom value (e.g. 0.0) if null.
Omitting partitionBy triggers a global window, collecting all data onto a single worker node (should be avoided at scale).
use_case: Calculating rolling account balances and identifying transaction recency for AML (Anti-Money Laundering) sequence reviews.

title: Complex Types: Structs, Arrays, and Maps
description: Working with nested schemas, lists, and key-value mapping structures natively in PySpark. This is key for parsing multi-valued JSON structures (like SWIFT/ISO20022 messages) without flattening them prematurely.
code:
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, struct, array, explode, map_keys

# 1. Nest columns into a Struct (useful for grouping metadata)
struct_df = silver_df.withColumn("audit_meta", struct(
    col("ingestion_ts").alias("loaded_at"),
    col("batch_id").alias("job_run_id")
))

# 2. Extract elements from an array structure using explode (row replication)
exploded_trades_df = raw_trades_df \
    .withColumn("trade_leg", explode("trade_legs")) \
    .select("trade_id", "counterparty", "trade_leg.leg_amount", "trade_leg.currency")

# 3. Work with maps to retrieve configuration properties
config_keys_df = app_configs_df.withColumn("keys", map_keys("property_map"))
notes: struct creates a single complex column containing sub-fields, accessible via dot-notation (col.subfield).
explode takes an array or map column and generates a new row for each element, replicating other column values.
higher-order functions (e.g. filter, transform) can process arrays inline without needing to explode first.
Maps are perfect for dynamic properties where schema keys change frequently across records.
use_case: Decomposing nested trade messages containing multiple execution legs into individual rows for capital risk metrics calculation.

title: Built-in Functions & Null Handling
description: Standard practices for cleaning dirty inputs, using conditional logic, and handling missing values safely. Resolving null values ensures accurate calculations in financial rollup reporting.
code:
from pyspark.sql.functions import coalesce, col, when, lit

# Clean customer profile details and assign defaults for reporting
sanitized_customers_df = customer_df.withColumn(
    "contact_phone", 
    coalesce(col("mobile_number"), col("home_phone"), lit("NOT_PROVIDED"))
).withColumn(
    "risk_tier_category",
    when(col("risk_score") >= 80, "HIGH")
    .when((col("risk_score") >= 40) & (col("risk_score") < 80), "MEDIUM")
    .otherwise("LOW")
)

# Fill null numeric amounts with zero and empty text with default
cleansed_df = sanitized_customers_df.na.fill({"credit_limit": 0.0, "country_code": "EU"})
notes: coalesce evaluates columns from left to right and returns the first non-null value.
when().otherwise() executes conditional switch logic, behaving like SQL CASE WHEN.
df.na.fill() fills null values selectively using a Python dictionary mapping column names to defaults.
Using lit() is required to supply literal values (e.g. 'NOT_PROVIDED') inside Spark expressions.
use_case: Resolving missing contact and rating details in credit applicant records prior to scoring modeling.

title: User Defined Functions (UDFs & Pandas UDFs)
description: Extending Spark functionality with custom Python functions. Distinguishes between standard row-by-row Python UDFs and vectorized Pandas UDFs (PyArrow) that perform calculations in batch.
notes: Standard Python UDFs suffer from serialization overhead because data is moved between the JVM and Python interpreter row by row.
Pandas UDFs use Apache Arrow to transfer data in batches, allowing high-performance vectorized operations.
Ensure PyArrow is installed and enabled (spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled = true) to run Pandas UDFs.
Type hinting in @pandas_udf is mandatory to define the return structure of the function.
use_case: Executing complex EU tax calculations on millions of invoice records inside Azure Databricks without JVM-to-Python bottlenecks.

title: Delta Time Travel & History
description: Querying historical versions of a Delta table using transaction log snapshots. This is essential for reconstructing past data states for auditing, debugging, and rollback.
code:
# 1. Retrieve the audit trail history of a Delta table
history_df = spark.read.format("delta") \
    .load("abfss://silver@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/ledger") \
    .history()

# 2. Query historical data as of version 5
df_version_5 = spark.read.format("delta") \
    .option("versionAsOf", "5") \
    .load("abfss://silver@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/ledger")

# 3. Query historical data as of a specific date and time
df_timestamp = spark.read.format("delta") \
    .option("timestampAsOf", "2026-01-01 12:00:00") \
    .load("abfss://silver@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/ledger")
notes: Delta Lake retains historical files based on table properties like logRetentionDuration and deletedFileRetentionDuration.
versionAsOf reads the specific commit file from the _delta_log directory.
timestampAsOf searches for the closest log commit timestamp that matches the criteria.
Time travel is read-only; to rollback, overwrite the active table with the historical version's contents.
use_case: Reconstructing monthly account balances as of a precise audit cut-off date to satisfy EBA regulatory inspectors.

title: Auto Loader (cloudFiles) for Streaming Ingestion
description: Incrementally and efficiently processing new files as they land in cloud storage (ADLS Gen2 / OneLake) without managing file lists. Auto Loader maintains state using RocksDB checkpoints.
code:
# Configure Auto Loader to stream incoming JSON transaction files
streaming_df = spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles") \
    .option("cloudFiles.format", "json") \
    .option("cloudFiles.schemaLocation", "abfss://meta@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/schemas/txns") \
    .option("cloudFiles.rescuedDataColumn", "_rescued_data") \
    .load("abfss://landing@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/incoming_files/*.json")

# Write the stream to a bronze Delta table using structured checkpointing
query = streaming_df.writeStream.format("delta") \
    .outputMode("append") \
    .option("checkpointLocation", "abfss://meta@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/checkpoints/txns") \
    .start("abfss://bronze@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/bronze_transactions")
notes: cloudFiles.schemaLocation is required to store the schema state and support schema evolution automatically.
rescuedDataColumn captures columns that do not match the schema, preserving corrupt data for auditing.
Auto Loader can scale to process billions of files using cloud notifications (SQS/Event Grid) or directory listing.
A checkpoint location is mandatory for streaming to guarantee exactly-once processing semantics.
use_case: Ingesting volatile and unstructured payment stream feeds continuously from landing zones to Bronze Delta layers.

title: Date and Time Manipulation
description: Standard functions for parsing, formatting, and arithmetic operations on dates and timestamps. Critical for defining reporting boundaries and calculating periods in compliance schedules.
code:
from pyspark.sql.functions import to_date, to_timestamp, date_add, date_trunc, date_format, col

# Parse string representations of dates, truncate to month, and format
datetime_df = raw_dates_df.select(
    col("txn_id"),
    to_timestamp(col("raw_timestamp"), "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSS").alias("txn_ts"),
    to_date(col("raw_date"), "dd/MM/yyyy").alias("txn_date")
).withColumn(
    "interest_calc_start", date_add(col("txn_date"), 30)
).withColumn(
    "fiscal_month", date_trunc("MM", col("txn_date"))
).withColumn(
    "report_year_week", date_format(col("txn_date"), "yyyy-w")
)

# Output schema verification
datetime_df.printSchema()
notes: Use to_date and to_timestamp with explicit format patterns (Java SimpleDateFormat) to avoid parsing failures.
date_trunc truncates dates/timestamps to a specified level like year ('YYYY'), month ('MM'), or hour ('HH').
date_format converts date columns to formatted strings, useful for generating report paths or partition names.
Operations automatically account for leap years and month lengths.
use_case: Normalizing heterogeneous date string formats from international payment gateways into a standardized ISO format.

title: Partitioning and Bucketing
description: Optimizing physical storage layout in cloud storage. Partitioning isolates data into folders based on low-cardinality keys, while bucketing divides data into fixed files based on high-cardinality keys to eliminate shuffles.
code:
# 1. Write DataFrame partitioned by transaction date (Low Cardinality)
transactions_df.write.format("delta") \
    .mode("append") \
    .partitionBy("txn_date") \
    .save("abfss://silver@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/partitioned_txns")

# 2. Write DataFrame bucketed by account ID (High Cardinality)
# Bucketing is saved as a managed table structure
transactions_df.write.format("parquet") \
    .mode("overwrite") \
    .bucketBy(100, "account_id") \
    .sortBy("txn_timestamp") \
    .saveAsTable("eu_bfsi_prod.silver.bucketed_txns")
notes: Partitioning is highly effective for filtering (partition pruning) on queries, but should not exceed 10,000 partitions to avoid directory scanning issues.
Liquid Clustering (Delta Lake DBR 13.3+) replaces static partitioning, resolving partition-drift performance issues.
bucketBy requires saveAsTable because metadata must be saved in the Spark metastore to let readers skip shuffles.
Use bucketing when you routinely perform joins or aggregations on high-cardinality columns (e.g. account_id).
use_case: Designing storage layout for credit transaction tables, using date-partitioning for analytical queries and account-bucketing for reconciliation joins.

title: Delta Lake MERGE INTO (Upsert Operations)
description: Atomic upsert (insert, update, delete) operations inside Delta tables. Crucial for syncing changing master datasets (e.g. customer dimensions) without rewriting whole directories.
code:
import logging

# Configure pipeline logger
logger = logging.getLogger("MedallionPipeline")

try:
    # Target Delta table representation
    target_table_path = "abfss://silver@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/customers"
    
    # Load source staging updates
    staging_updates_df = spark.read.format("delta").load("abfss://bronze@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/customer_updates")
    
    from delta.tables import DeltaTable
    
    # Instantiate the target DeltaTable object
    delta_target = DeltaTable.forPath(spark, target_table_path)
    
    # Execute the upsert (merge) statement
    delta_target.alias("t").merge(
        source=staging_updates_df.alias("s"),
        condition="t.customer_id == s.customer_id"
    ).whenMatchedUpdate(set={
        "t.customer_name": "s.customer_name",
        "t.email": "s.email",
        "t.risk_score": "s.risk_score",
        "t.updated_ts": "s.updated_ts"
    }).whenNotMatchedInsert(values={
        "customer_id": "s.customer_id",
        "customer_name": "s.customer_name",
        "email": "s.email",
        "risk_score": "s.risk_score",
        "created_ts": "s.updated_ts",
        "updated_ts": "s.updated_ts"
    }).execute()
except Exception as e:
    logger.error(f"Pipeline stage failed in Delta Lake MERGE INTO (Upsert Operations): {str(e)}")
    raise
notes: MERGE INTO matches rows between target and source based on a join condition, applying updates or insertions.
Delta Lake ensures that the merge is transactional; readers see either the old state or the full new state.
Optimize performance by ensuring the merge key column is clustered (Z-Ordered) on the target table.
Add additional conditions (e.g. whenMatchedUpdate(condition='s.updated_ts > t.updated_ts')) to prevent out-of-order overrides.
use_case: Updating customer master profiles in the Silver layer (SCD Type 1) with incoming daily profile drift updates.

title: Delta Lake Change Data Feed (CDF)
description: Enabling and querying row-level change propagation logs in Delta tables. Allows incremental extraction of changes (inserts, updates, deletes) to populate downstream Gold aggregates efficiently.
code:
import logging

# Configure pipeline logger
logger = logging.getLogger("MedallionPipeline")

try:
    # 1. Read change feed events between two versions of the Silver customer table
    cdf_df = spark.read.format("delta") \
        .option("readChangeFeed", "true") \
        .option("startingVersion", 10) \
        .option("endingVersion", 15) \
        .load("abfss://silver@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/customers")
    
    # 2. Filter CDF events to extract modifications and propagate to audit ledger
    updates_and_deletes_df = cdf_df.filter(
        col("_change_type").isin("update_postimage", "delete")
    ).select(
        col("customer_id"),
        col("risk_score"),
        col("_change_type").alias("operation_type"),
        col("_commit_timestamp").alias("applied_at")
    )
except Exception as e:
    logger.error(f"Pipeline stage failed in Delta Lake Change Data Feed (CDF): {str(e)}")
    raise
notes: CDF must be explicitly enabled on the table via table properties: tblproperties('delta.enableChangeDataFeed' = 'true').
Special metadata columns returned include _change_type, _commit_version, and _commit_timestamp.
_change_type values include insert, delete, update_preimage (value before update), and update_postimage (value after update).
CDF eliminates the need for expensive full-table diff comparison scans in multi-hop medallion updates.
use_case: Propagating KYC risk rating status changes incrementally from the Silver customer directory to Gold aggregate tables.

title: Broadcast Join & Joins Optimization
description: Eliminating network shuffle stages when joining a large table with a small reference dataset. PySpark copies the small dataset to all worker executors, keeping the join entirely local.
code:
import logging

# Configure pipeline logger
logger = logging.getLogger("MedallionPipeline")

try:
    from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast
    
    # Load the massive transactions dataset (10 Billion records)
    txns_df = spark.read.format("delta").load("abfss://silver@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/transactions")
    
    # Load small currency dimension table (100 rows)
    currency_dim_df = spark.read.format("delta").load("abfss://silver@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/currencies")
    
    # Force broadcast join of the currency dimension
    enriched_txns_df = txns_df.join(
        broadcast(currency_dim_df),
        on="currency_code",
        how="inner"
    )
    
    # Verify execution plan contains 'BroadcastHashJoin' using explain()
    enriched_txns_df.explain()
except Exception as e:
    logger.error(f"Pipeline stage failed in Broadcast Join & Joins Optimization: {str(e)}")
    raise
notes: Broadcast joins bypass Shuffle operations, which are the most expensive resource bottleneck in Spark.
The default maximum size for a broadcasted table is 10MB (spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold).
Broadcasting a large table can trigger OutOfMemory (OOM) errors on Spark worker executors.
Check query plans for 'BroadcastHashJoin' vs 'SortMergeJoin' to verify optimization success.
use_case: Joining billions of retail transactions with a tiny, static currency exchange rate lookup table during close-of-day valuation.

title: Caching and Persistence Strategies
description: Caching intermediate DataFrames in executor memory or disk. This avoids re-evaluating long execution lineages when the same DataFrame is accessed multiple times by downstream actions.
code:
import logging

# Configure pipeline logger
logger = logging.getLogger("MedallionPipeline")

try:
    from pyspark import StorageLevel
    
    # Load and apply heavy transformations to expose transaction flags
    flagged_accounts_df = raw_txns \
        .filter(col("amount_eur") > 250000) \
        .groupBy("account_id").count() \
        .filter(col("count") >= 5)
    
    # Persist to memory and serialized disk spill (retains resource availability)
    flagged_accounts_df.persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK_SER)
    
    # Trigger action 1: Count of critical warning accounts
    high_risk_count = flagged_accounts_df.count()
    
    # Trigger action 2: Save list to audit files (reuses the cached state)
    flagged_accounts_df.write.format("delta").save("abfss://gold@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/aml_targets")
    
    # Always unpersist to release memory when transactions are completed
    flagged_accounts_df.unpersist()
except Exception as e:
    logger.error(f"Pipeline stage failed in Caching and Persistence Strategies: {str(e)}")
    raise
notes: cache() is a shortcut for persist() using default StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK.
Use serialized persistence (MEMORY_AND_DISK_SER) to reduce memory foot-print and garbage collection overhead.
Caching is lazy; it only materializes in memory when the first action (e.g. count, write) is executed.
Always unpersist() DataFrames to prevent cluster memory leak issues on shared interactive workspaces.
use_case: Caching a filtered daily risk exposure dataset reused across three different reporting pipelines (AML, credit risk, regulatory reporting).

title: Custom Spark Partitioning & Repartitioning
description: Managing the degree of parallelism and layout of partitions in memory. Explains the performance trade-offs between shuffle-inducing repartition and metadata-only coalesce.
code:
import logging

# Configure pipeline logger
logger = logging.getLogger("MedallionPipeline")

try:
    # Load Silver transactions (poorly partitioned on landing)
    dirty_input_df = spark.read.format("delta").load("abfss://bronze@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/landing_txns")
    
    # 1. repartition: Increase partitions and shuffle data evenly across keys
    # Useful to increase parallelism for heavy CPU tasks
    repartitioned_df = dirty_input_df.repartition(100, "account_id")
    
    # 2. coalesce: Decreases partitions without shuffling (minimizes data movement)
    # Ideal for merging small partitions before writing target files
    optimized_for_export_df = repartitioned_df.filter(col("amount_eur") > 10000) \
        .coalesce(5)
    
    # Write output (will produce exactly 5 files in storage)
    optimized_for_export_df.write.format("json").save("abfss://export@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/daily_alerts")
except Exception as e:
    logger.error(f"Pipeline stage failed in Custom Spark Partitioning & Repartitioning: {str(e)}")
    raise
notes: repartition() triggers a full shuffle to distribute data evenly, creating equal-sized partitions.
coalesce() only collapses partitions on the same executor, avoiding network shuffles entirely.
Calling repartition() with a partition column optimizes execution paths for downstream grouping.
Coalescing to 1 file before writing causes a bottlenecks, as the final step runs on a single worker executor.
use_case: Balancing cluster work (100 partitions during parallel mapping) and merging reports (5 files during export writes).

title: Handling Skewed Data with Salting
description: Resolving performance bottlenecks caused by uneven data distribution. By appending a randomized suffix (salt key) to skewed keys, transactions are distributed evenly across executors during joins.
code:
import logging

# Configure pipeline logger
logger = logging.getLogger("MedallionPipeline")

try:
    from pyspark.sql.functions import col, concat, lit, rand, round, explode, array
    
    # Target Table: Massive transactions table where some account IDs are extremely skewed (e.g. corporate accounts)
    # Reference Table: Accounts dimension table
    
    # 1. Salt the transactions DataFrame by adding a random salt column (0-9)
    salt_factor = 10
    salted_txns_df = txns_df.withColumn("salt", round(rand() * (salt_factor - 1))) \
        .withColumn("salted_join_key", concat(col("account_id"), lit("_"), col("salt")))
    
    # 2. Replicate the accounts dimension table 10 times to match all possible salts
    exploded_salts_df = spark.range(0, salt_factor).withColumnRenamed("id", "salt")
    replicated_accounts_df = accounts_df.crossJoin(exploded_salts_df) \
        .withColumn("salted_join_key", concat(col("account_id"), lit("_"), col("salt")))
    
    # 3. Perform skew-free join on salted keys
    skew_free_join_df = salted_txns_df.join(
        replicated_accounts_df,
        on="salted_join_key",
        how="inner"
    ).drop("salt", "salted_join_key")
except Exception as e:
    logger.error(f"Pipeline stage failed in Handling Skewed Data with Salting: {str(e)}")
    raise
notes: Data skew manifests in the Spark UI as a single task taking significantly longer than others (straggler task).
Salting breaks down the massive group corresponding to a skewed key into smaller subsets that run in parallel.
The salt factor determines how many times the dimension table is replicated; choose a value that balances JVM memory limits.
Spark 3.x Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) can handle skew auto-detection dynamically using shuffle statistics.
use_case: Joining billions of payment rows with account masters when corporate ledger accounts hold millions of events compared to retail accounts holding tens of events.

title: GDPR Compliance & Dynamic Data Masking
description: Enforcing security configurations dynamically on PII columns and complying with the GDPR 'Right to be Forgotten' by purging targeted personal details across historical snapshots without compromising table ACID logs.
code:
import logging

# Configure pipeline logger
logger = logging.getLogger("MedallionPipeline")

try:
    from pyspark.sql.functions import when, expr, col, sha2, lit
    
    # 1. Dynamic Column Masking: Obfuscate IBAN for unauthorized users
    # is_member evaluates the active caller's Microsoft Entra ID groups in Unity Catalog
    secured_customer_df = customer_raw_df.withColumn(
        "iban_secured",
        when(expr("is_member('Compliance_Auditors')"), col("iban"))
        .when(expr("is_member('Standard_Developers')"), sha2(col("iban"), 256))
        .otherwise(lit("ACCESS_DENIED"))
    )
    
    # 2. Right to be Forgotten (GDPR Article 17): Purge records based on customer requests
    # Perform deletion in the Delta table and clean up history using VACUUM
    spark.sql("DELETE FROM eu_bfsi_prod.silver.customers WHERE customer_id = 'CUST-EU-8809'")
    
    # Run VACUUM to permanently purge deleted data files from physical storage
    # Set retention to 0 hours for immediate physical delete (requires bypass flag)
    spark.conf.set("spark.databricks.delta.vacuum.parallelDelete.enabled", "true")
    spark.sql("SET spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled = false")
    spark.sql("VACUUM eu_bfsi_prod.silver.customers RETAIN 0 HOURS")
except Exception as e:

    raise

title: Idempotent Medallion Pipeline Orchestration
description: Designing end-to-end batch and micro-batch data pipelines that guarantee exactly-once delivery, avoiding data duplication during job reruns or mid-execution failures.
code:
import logging

# Configure pipeline logger
logger = logging.getLogger("MedallionPipeline")

try:
    from pyspark.sql import functions as F
    
    # Batch Ingestion pattern with explicit batch tracking
    def ingest_daily_transactions(batch_date: str, source_path: str, target_table: str):
        # 1. Load batch files for the specific execution date
        batch_df = spark.read.format("delta").load(source_path) \
            .filter(F.col("txn_date") == batch_date)
        
        # 2. Add pipeline metadata for audit tracing
        enriched_batch_df = batch_df \
            .withColumn("_pipeline_batch_id", F.lit(batch_date)) \
            .withColumn("_ingested_at", F.current_timestamp())
    
        # 3. Idempotently write to target table using INSERT OVERWRITE on the target partition
        # Rerunning this function for the same date will safely overwrite without doubling rows
        enriched_batch_df.write.format("delta") \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .option("replaceWhere", f"txn_date = '{batch_date}'") \
            .save(target_table)
except Exception as e:
    logger.error(f"Pipeline stage failed in Idempotent Medallion Pipeline Orchestration: {str(e)}")
    raise
notes: Idempotency ensures that executing a pipeline multiple times with the same input produces the exact same output.
Using option('replaceWhere', ...) ensures Spark only overwrites files within matching partitions.
Avoid append mode without duplicate validation since running twice will create duplicates.
For streaming workloads, exactly-once is enforced using checkpoints and state databases (RocksDB).
use_case: Orchestrating daily transaction ingestion schedules from payment landing zones to the Silver layer that are resilient to pipeline failures.

title: ACID Transactions and Concurrent Writes
description: Managing concurrent transactions and resolving conflicts. Delta Lake uses Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) to handle parallel write operations, failing transactions only if they try to modify the same partitions.
code:
import logging

# Configure pipeline logger
logger = logging.getLogger("MedallionPipeline")

try:
    # Scenario: Simultaneously streaming alerts into gold table and running background maintenance delete
    from delta.tables import DeltaTable
    
    # Background process deleting expired transactions
    def run_purging_operation():
        try:
            # Perform logical delete on target
            spark.sql("DELETE FROM eu_bfsi_prod.gold.compliance_ledger WHERE txn_date < '2019-01-01'")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"Conflict detected: {e}")
            # OCC conflict throws 'ConcurrentAppendException' or 'WriteConflictException'
    
    # Stream write configuration with concurrency limits
    # Enable schema evolution and configure write limits
    spark.conf.set("spark.databricks.delta.write.allowConcurrentWrites", "true")
    spark.conf.set("spark.databricks.delta.properties.defaults.isolationLevel", "WriteSerializable")
except Exception as e:
    logger.error(f"Pipeline stage failed in ACID Transactions and Concurrent Writes: {str(e)}")
    raise
notes: Optimistic Concurrency Control assumes writes rarely conflict; it validates before commit and retries if a conflict occurs.
Isolation levels: 'Serializable' guarantees full transaction isolation; 'WriteSerializable' allows parallel updates to different partitions.

Design target partitions carefully; writing to different date-partitions (e.g. 2026-05-31 vs 2026-05-30) prevents concurrent conflicts.

title: Deduplication Retaining Latest Timestamp via Window Functions
description: Deterministically removes duplicate records for an entity by ranking rows based on timestamp descending and filtering for rank 1.
code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

# Sample dataset with customer updates
data = [
    ("cust_101", "2026-10-01 10:00:00", "Logged In"),
    ("cust_101", "2026-10-01 14:30:00", "Purchased Item"),  # Latest for 101
    ("cust_102", "2026-10-01 09:15:00", "Added to Cart"),
    ("cust_102", "2026-10-01 09:00:00", "Viewed Page")
]
df = spark.createDataFrame(data, ["customer_id", "event_time", "activity"])

# Define partition window ordered by event_time descending
window_spec = Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy(F.col("event_time").desc())

# Assign row number and retain only the latest record
df_latest = df.withColumn("row_num", F.row_number().over(window_spec)) \
    .filter(F.col("row_num") == 1) \
    .drop("row_num")

df_latest.show(truncate=False)
notes: Avoid using dropDuplicates(['customer_id']) when you need the most recent row, as dropDuplicates drops non-deterministically.
Add a secondary column in orderBy() to break exact timestamp ties consistently.

)

# Step 2: Explode the lookup table across matching salt range [0..3]

df_lookup_salted = df_lookup.crossJoin(salt_df) \

title: Delta Lake SCD Type 2 Dimension Upsert via MERGE INTO
description: Performs an atomic SCD Type 2 dimension merge, expiring outdated records and inserting active versions with effective dates in a single transaction.
code:
from delta.tables import DeltaTable
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

target_table = DeltaTable.forName(spark, "dim_customer")

# Prepare staged updates with dummy null keys to trigger both update & insert
staged_updates = df_updates.select(
    F.col("customer_id").alias("merge_key"),
    F.col("*")
).unionByName(
    df_updates.select(F.lit(None).alias("merge_key"), F.col("*"))
)

# Atomic Merge execution
target_table.alias("t").merge(
    source=staged_updates.alias("s"),
    condition="t.customer_id = s.merge_key AND t.is_current = true"
).whenMatchedUpdate(
    condition="t.city <> s.city OR t.segment <> s.segment",
    set={"is_current": "false", "end_date": "current_timestamp()"}
).whenNotMatchedInsert(
    values={
        "customer_id": "s.customer_id",
        "name": "s.name",
        "city": "s.city",
        "segment": "s.segment",
        "is_current": "true",
        "start_date": "current_timestamp()",
        "end_date": "null"
    }
).execute()
notes: The union with a null merge_key forces Spark to match active records for expiration while also triggering the insert branch for new records.
Guarantees ACID transactional consistency with zero duplicate active records.
use_case: Historical dimension tracking in enterprise data warehouses and lakehouses.

title: Object-Oriented Dynamic PySpark Transformation Utility

title: Benchmarking 6 Delta Lake Optimization Levers at Scale
description: Hands-on empirical benchmarking comparing 6 Delta Lake layout and file management techniques (Baseline small files, Physical Partitioning, Z-Ordering, Manual Compaction, Auto Optimize, and Liquid Clustering) across a 50M-row dataset, measuring scan time, input files, and bytes read via the Spark UI.
code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
import pyspark.sql.functions as F
from pyspark.sql.functions import col

spark = SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate()
CATALOG = "delta_opt"
SCHEMA = "sales"

# 1. Baseline unoptimized table with fragmented small files
# spark.sql(f"CREATE TABLE {CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.sales_raw ...")

# 2. Physical Partitioning (low-cardinality country column)
df_raw = spark.table(f"{CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.sales_raw")
df_raw.write.format("delta") \
    .mode("overwrite") \
    .partitionBy("country") \
    .saveAsTable(f"{CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.sales_partitioned")

# 3. Multi-dimensional Z-Ordering on high-cardinality keys
spark.sql(f"""
    CREATE TABLE {CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.sales_zorder AS 
    SELECT * FROM {CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.sales_raw;
""")
spark.sql(f"OPTIMIZE {CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.sales_zorder ZORDER BY (customer_id, product_id)")

# 4. Liquid Clustering (modern recommended standard - Hilbert curve)
spark.sql(f"""
    CREATE TABLE {CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.sales_liquid 
    USING DELTA 
    CLUSTER BY (sale_date, customer_id)
    AS SELECT * FROM {CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.sales_raw;
""")
# Incrementally clusters new appends without full-table rewrites
spark.sql(f"OPTIMIZE {CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.sales_liquid")

# 5. Profile metrics in Spark UI & metadata
detail_df = spark.sql(f"DESCRIBE DETAIL {CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.sales_liquid")
detail_df.select("numFiles", "sizeInBytes", "clusteringColumns").show()
notes: Liquid Clustering replaces both partitioning and Z-Order, supporting dynamic clustering key alterations.
Z-Ordering is effective for multi-column queries on legacy tables but suffers from high write amplification on frequent appends.
Physical partitioning on high-cardinality columns (>10,000 values) leads to severe small-file sprawl and metadata overhead.
Use DESCRIBE DETAIL to verify file count reduction and average file size approaching the ~1GB sweet spot.
use_case: Optimizing a 50M-row retail sales fact table in Databricks to eliminate query scan bottlenecks and compare empirical performance across layout strategies.

title: Event-Time Watermarking & Windowed Stateful Aggregations
description: Implements event-time stateful streaming aggregations with watermarking to handle out-of-order and late data cleanly. Uses tumbling and sliding windows with state eviction to prevent executor out-of-memory errors.
code:
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, window, sum, count

# Read clickstream events from Kafka or Delta Bronze
events_df = spark.readStream.format("delta").table("bronze.clickstream")

# Define 10-minute watermark for late data handling
windowed_metrics = events_df \
    .withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes") \
    .groupBy(
        window(col("event_time"), "1 hour", "15 minutes"), # Sliding 1-hr window every 15 mins
        col("campaign_id"),
        col("country")
    ) \
    .agg(
        count("click_id").alias("total_clicks"),
        sum("conversion_value").alias("gross_revenue")
    )

# Write to Silver Gold aggregated layer with Update output mode
query = windowed_metrics.writeStream \
    .format("delta") \
    .outputMode("update") \
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/mnt/checkpoints/campaign_hourly_metrics") \
    .toTable("silver.campaign_hourly_metrics")

query.awaitTermination()
notes: withWatermark('event_time', '10 minutes') instructs Spark that events arriving older than 10 mins past current max event time can be dropped.
Watermarking is mandatory for stateful streaming operations to allow the RocksDB/HDFS state store to purge expired state buffers.
Update mode writes only updated aggregate windows per micro-batch, whereas Append mode emits only finalized closed windows.
Sliding windows (duration, slide) allow tracking moving trends with overlapping time boundaries.
use_case: Tracking real-time ad campaign conversions and revenue in sliding 1-hour windows while bounding state store memory usage.

title: foreachBatch Idempotent Upsert & Deduplication Pattern
description: Production pattern using foreachBatch to execute multi-table writes and ACID MERGE INTO operations within a streaming pipeline. Solves duplicate delivery issues in streaming CDC pipelines using batch deduplication.
code:
from delta.tables import DeltaTable
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, row_number
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

target_delta = DeltaTable.forName(spark, "silver.customer_accounts")

def process_micro_batch(micro_batch_df, batch_id):
    # 1. Deduplicate within the micro-batch window (take latest updated record)
    window_spec = Window.partitionBy("account_id").orderBy(col("last_modified_ts").desc())
    deduped_batch = micro_batch_df \
        .withColumn("row_num", row_number().over(window_spec)) \
        .filter(col("row_num") == 1) \
        .drop("row_num")
        
    # 2. Idempotent MERGE into Target Silver Delta Table
    target_delta.alias("tgt").merge(
        deduped_batch.alias("src"),
        "tgt.account_id = src.account_id"
    ).whenMatchedUpdate(
        condition="src.last_modified_ts > tgt.last_modified_ts",
        set={
            "balance": "src.balance",
            "status": "src.status",
            "last_modified_ts": "src.last_modified_ts"
        }
    ).whenNotMatchedInsert(
        values={
            "account_id": "src.account_id",
            "balance": "src.balance",
            "status": "src.status",
            "created_ts": "src.last_modified_ts",
            "last_modified_ts": "src.last_modified_ts"
        }
    ).execute()

# Stream processor calling foreachBatch
streaming_query = spark.readStream.table("bronze.cdc_accounts") \
    .writeStream \
    .foreachBatch(process_micro_batch) \
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/mnt/checkpoints/accounts_upsert") \
    .start()

streaming_query.awaitTermination()
notes: foreachBatch allows applying arbitrary batch operations (like DeltaTable.merge) to streaming micro-batch DataFrames.
Batch deduplication with Window.partitionBy ensures multiple CDC updates for the same key in one micro-batch don't cause MERGE conflict errors.
Provides end-to-end exactly-once idempotent semantics even when micro-batches are re-executed upon cluster failure.
Enables updating multiple target tables (e.g. Silver fact + quarantine audit table) in a single streaming job.
use_case: Consuming real-time banking CDC account updates from Kafka into a Silver dimensional table without duplicate record conflicts.

title: Databricks Genie Space Setup & Star Schema Optimization
description: Architecting and calibrating a Databricks Genie AI/BI space on top of a Kimball dimensional star schema (Sales Fact, Customer Dim, Product Dim, Date Dim), defining semantic instructions, benchmark evaluation questions, and trusted SQL definitions.
code:
# Databricks Genie Space Semantic Configuration Pattern
# 1. Ensure Star Schema tables have rich column comments and PRIMARY/FOREIGN keys in Unity Catalog:
spark.sql("""
    ALTER TABLE gold.fct_sales 
    ALTER COLUMN customer_id COMMENT 'Unique foreign key referencing dim_customer.customer_id';
""")

# 2. Informational Primary & Foreign Key constraints help Genie resolve join paths accurately:
spark.sql("""
    ALTER TABLE gold.dim_customer ADD CONSTRAINT pk_dim_customer PRIMARY KEY (customer_id);
    ALTER TABLE gold.fct_sales ADD CONSTRAINT fk_sales_customer FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES gold.dim_customer(customer_id);
""")

# 3. Genie Space Semantic Instructions (YAML / System Prompt specification):
genie_space_config = {
    "space_name": "Executive Sales Analytics Space",
    "tables": ["gold.fct_sales", "gold.dim_customer", "gold.dim_product", "gold.dim_date"],
    "general_instructions": """
        - Always join fct_sales with dim_date on date_id to filter by calendar year and quarter.
        - 'Revenue' or 'Sales' refers to SUM(net_amount), excluding tax and shipping fees.
        - 'Active Customers' refers to COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) with at least 1 order in the period.
        - Format currency outputs to 2 decimal places.
        - Never generate CROSS JOIN; always use explicit foreign key relationships.
    """,
    "certified_sql_queries": [
        {
            "question": "What is the top-selling product category by revenue this quarter?",
            "verified_sql": """
                SELECT p.category_name, SUM(f.net_amount) AS total_revenue
                FROM gold.fct_sales f
                JOIN gold.dim_product p ON f.product_id = p.product_id
                JOIN gold.dim_date d ON f.date_id = d.date_id
                WHERE d.quarter = '2026-Q3'
                GROUP BY p.category_name
                ORDER BY total_revenue DESC LIMIT 5;
            """
        }
    ]
}
notes: Genie spaces leverage Unity Catalog table comments, column descriptions, and informational PK/FK constraints to infer join paths.
Providing certified SQL query pairs anchors the underlying foundation model to verified business metric logic.
Clear natural language synonyms in instructions prevent hallucinations on domain acronyms like ARR, NRR, or GMV.
Run benchmark suites across 20-50 business questions to measure deterministic Text-to-SQL accuracy.

title: Production Auto Loader Streaming with Rescued Data
description: Ingesting high-volume file streams using Databricks Auto Loader (cloudFiles) with dynamic schema evolution and a dedicated _rescued_data column to prevent pipeline breakage from corrupted or schema-deviant records.
code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# 1. Configure Auto Loader stream with schema evolution & rescue mechanism
raw_stream = (
    spark.readStream
    .format("cloudFiles")
    .option("cloudFiles.format", "json")
    .option("cloudFiles.schemaLocation", "/Volumes/prod_catalog/checkpoints/orders_schema/")
    .option("cloudFiles.inferColumnTypes", "true")
    .option("cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode", "addNewColumns")
    .option("cloudFiles.rescuedDataColumn", "_rescued_data")
    .option("cloudFiles.maxFilesPerTrigger", 500)  # Rate limiting backpressure
    .load("/Volumes/prod_catalog/landing/raw_orders/")
)

# 2. Add audit timestamp and monitor corrupted records
audited_stream = (
    raw_stream
    .withColumn("ingestion_ts", F.current_timestamp())
    .withColumn("is_corrupted", F.col("_rescued_data").isNotNull())
)

# 3. Write micro-batch to Bronze Delta Lake table with checkpointing
query = (
    audited_stream
    .writeStream
    .format("delta")
    .outputMode("append")
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/Volumes/prod_catalog/checkpoints/orders_delta_write/")
    .trigger(availableNow=True)  # Incremental batch trigger
    .toTable("prod_catalog.bronze.orders_raw")
)
notes: Auto Loader automatically discovers new files as they arrive in cloud object storage via incremental directory listing or SNS/SQS event notifications.
The _rescued_data column captures values with type mismatches or unparsed tokens, preventing pipeline termination.
trigger(availableNow=True) processes all available data in multiple micro-batches then stops the cluster, saving compute costs vs continuous streaming.
Always store checkpoints on durable, separate cloud storage to guarantee exactly-once processing across pipeline restarts.
use_case: Building production landing-zone pipelines that ingest millions of semi-structured supplier JSON files daily into Bronze Delta tables without failing on unanticipated schema changes.

title: Programmatic DeltaTable MERGE (SCD Type 2 & Deletions)
description: Executing programmatic Delta Lake merge operations using DeltaTable.forName() in PySpark. Demonstrates multi-branch conditional updates, soft deletions, and inserts with predicate pruning for high performance.
code:
from delta.tables import DeltaTable
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# 1. Reference target Delta Lake table
delta_target = DeltaTable.forName(spark, "prod_catalog.silver.customer_dim")

# 2. Incoming batch with updates, inserts, and soft-delete flags
updates_df = spark.read.table("prod_catalog.staging.customer_updates")

# 3. Execute atomic MERGE INTO
(
    delta_target.alias("target")
    .merge(
        updates_df.alias("source"),
        # Primary key match condition
        "target.customer_id = source.customer_id"
    )
    # Branch 1: Soft-delete when flagged by upstream system
    .whenMatchedUpdate(
        condition="source.is_deleted = true",
        set={
            "is_active": F.lit(False),
            "updated_at": F.current_timestamp()
        }
    )
    # Branch 2: Update existing active records when source has newer timestamp
    .whenMatchedUpdate(
        condition="source.update_timestamp > target.updated_at",
        set={
            "email": "source.email",
            "phone": "source.phone",
            "tier": "source.tier",
            "updated_at": "source.update_timestamp"
        }
    )
    # Branch 3: Insert new customer records
    .whenNotMatchedInsert(
        values={
            "customer_id": "source.customer_id",
            "email": "source.email",
            "phone": "source.phone",
            "tier": "source.tier",
            "is_active": F.lit(True),
            "created_at": F.current_timestamp(),
            "updated_at": "source.update_timestamp"
        }
    )
    .execute()
)
notes: DeltaTable.merge() executes atomically under Optimistic Concurrency Control.
Including partition columns in the merge condition enables partition pruning, skipping 90%+ of Parquet file scans.
Delta Lake 2.0+ supports multiple whenMatched and whenNotMatched clauses for complex conditional routing.
Avoid full table scans by ensuring target table has statistics computed and Liquid Clustering enabled on join keys.
use_case: Synchronizing customer master records from Salesforce and CRM systems into Silver dimension tables with audit tracking, soft-deletes, and timestamp fencing.

title: Higher-Order Functions on Complex Nested Arrays
description: Transforming, filtering, and aggregating complex nested arrays in-place using PySpark higher-order functions (transform, filter, aggregate). Eliminates expensive explode and re-group shuffles.
code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# Sample orders with nested array of line item structs
orders_df = spark.table("prod_catalog.silver.orders")

# 1. Transform: Apply 15% discount to all line item prices in-place
discounted_df = orders_df.withColumn(
    "discounted_items",
    F.transform(
        "line_items",
        lambda item: F.struct(
            item.item_id.alias("item_id"),
            item.quantity.alias("quantity"),
            F.round(item.unit_price * 0.85, 2).alias("unit_price")
        )
    )
)

# 2. Filter: Keep only line items where item quantity > 3
bulk_orders_df = discounted_df.withColumn(
    "bulk_items",
    F.filter("line_items", lambda item: item.quantity > 3)
)

# 3. Aggregate: Calculate total order weight by summing array items
weighted_orders_df = bulk_orders_df.withColumn(
    "total_order_weight_kg",
    F.aggregate(
        "line_items",
        F.lit(0.0), # Initial accumulator value
        lambda acc, item: acc + (item.quantity * item.unit_weight_kg)
    )
)

# 4. Check if any line item contains specific hazardous SKU
hazardous_df = weighted_orders_df.withColumn(
    "has_hazardous_materials",
    F.exists("line_items", lambda item: item.is_hazardous == True)
)
notes: Higher-order functions execute within Catalyst expression trees without unpacking arrays into separate rows.
Replacing explode() + groupBy() with transform() and aggregate() avoids multi-gigabyte shuffle spills.
Works seamlessly with deeply nested JSON structures, telemetry packets, and eCommerce shopping carts.
F.exists() short-circuits evaluation as soon as the first matching element is encountered in the array.
use_case: Processing complex eCommerce shopping carts containing hundreds of nested line items, computing shipping weights and category discounts with zero shuffle serialization.

title: Two-Phase Key Salting for Severe Join Skew Remediation
description: Resolving catastrophic join skew where a single key (e.g., country_code = 'US' or store_id = 'ONLINE') contains 80%+ of total records, stalling worker nodes on straggler tasks. Uses randomized two-phase salting.
code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

SALT_FACTOR = 16  # Distribute skewed key across 16 parallel tasks

fact_transactions = spark.table("prod_catalog.silver.transactions")
dim_stores = spark.table("prod_catalog.silver.dim_stores")

# Step 1: Add randomized salt [0..15] to large fact table
salted_fact = fact_transactions.withColumn(
    "salt_id",
    F.floor(F.rand() * SALT_FACTOR)
).withColumn(
    "salted_join_key",
    F.concat(F.col("store_id"), F.lit("_"), F.col("salt_id"))
)

# Step 2: Replicate dimension table records across all 16 salt IDs [0..15]
salt_table = spark.range(0, SALT_FACTOR).withColumnRenamed("id", "salt_id")
replicated_dim = dim_stores.crossJoin(salt_table).withColumn(
    "salted_join_key",
    F.concat(F.col("store_id"), F.lit("_"), F.col("salt_id"))
)

# Step 3: Perform balanced inner join on the salted key
balanced_joined_df = (
    salted_fact.join(replicated_dim, on="salted_join_key", how="inner")
    .drop("salted_join_key", "salt_id")
)

# Step 4: Validate execution plan: tasks finish uniformly without stragglers
balanced_joined_df.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("prod_catalog.gold.balanced_sales")
notes: Salting breaks monolithic partitions into multiple smaller, evenly distributed shuffle buckets.
Only apply salting to the specific skewed key; salting already uniform keys introduces unnecessary cross-join overhead.
Ensure Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) skew join is enabled (spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled = true) as first line of defense.
Replicating small dimension tables by 16x is trivial in memory compared to the cost of a 4-hour stuck shuffle stage.
use_case: Joining a 2-billion-row retail transactions dataset with store metadata where the e-commerce flagship store represents 85% of volume, preventing executor OOM and task stragglers.

title: Stateful Streaming Deduplication with Watermarking
description: Managing streaming state stores with event-time watermarking to execute stateful streaming deduplication without unbounded memory bloat. Configured with RocksDB state store for mission-critical reliability.
code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# 1. Enable RocksDB state store to avoid Java heap memory limits on high-state streams
spark.conf.set(
    "spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass",
    "org.apache.spark.sql.execution.streaming.state.RocksDBStateStoreProvider"
)

# 2. Read real-time telemetry stream from Azure Event Hubs / Kafka
telemetry_stream = (
    spark.readStream
    .format("delta")
    .table("prod_catalog.bronze.iot_telemetry_raw")
)

# 3. Define 2-hour watermark and deduplicate on device_id + event_time
deduplicated_stream = (
    telemetry_stream
    .withWatermark("event_timestamp", "2 hours")
    .dropDuplicates(["device_id", "event_timestamp"])
)

# 4. Windowed stateful aggregation: 10-minute tumbling windows
windowed_metrics = (
    deduplicated_stream
    .groupBy(
        F.window("event_timestamp", "10 minutes"),
        "device_type"
    )
    .agg(
        F.avg("temperature").alias("avg_temp"),
        F.max("vibration").alias("max_vibration"),
        F.count("event_id").alias("reading_count")
    )
)

# 5. Output to Silver Delta table with checkpointing
query = (
    windowed_metrics
    .writeStream
    .format("delta")
    .outputMode("append")
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/Volumes/prod_catalog/checkpoints/iot_silver_state/")
    .trigger(processingTime="1 minute")
    .toTable("prod_catalog.silver.iot_aggregated_metrics")
)
notes: Watermarking tells the state store when late data can be safely dropped and state purged from disk/memory.
Default HDFS-backed state store keeps state in JVM heap; RocksDB offloads state to local SSD, supporting tens of millions of active keys.
dropDuplicates with a watermark requires the watermark column to be present in the deduplication key set.
Append output mode only emits rows once the window falls behind the active watermark threshold.
use_case: Processing continuous streams of 50,000 IoT sensor events per second, filtering out redundant retry packets and computing 10-minute metrics with zero JVM heap exhaustion.

]

df_raw.show(truncate=False)

# --- Execution Step ---
# 1. Cleanse raw_amount by stripping non-numeric characters (except period)
clean_amount_expr = F.regexp_replace(F.col("raw_amount"), r"[^\d.]", "")

# 2. Apply safe casting: if sanitized string is empty or invalid, evaluate to NULL
df_cleansed = df_raw.withColumn(
    "clean_amount",
    F.when(clean_amount_expr == "", None).otherwise(clean_amount_expr.cast(T.DoubleType()))
)

# 3. Standardize timestamp handling
df_typed = df_cleansed.withColumn(
    "txn_timestamp",
    F.coalesce(
        F.to_timestamp(F.col("raw_timestamp"), "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss"),
        F.to_timestamp(F.col("raw_timestamp"), "dd/MM/yyyy HH:mm"),
        F.to_timestamp(F.col("raw_timestamp"), "yyyy-MM-dd")
    )
)

df_typed.show(truncate=False)

# --- Execution Step ---
# Valid records have both parsed amount and parsed timestamp
df_valid = df_typed.filter(F.col("clean_amount").isNotNull() & F.col("txn_timestamp").isNotNull())
df_quarantine = df_typed.filter(F.col("clean_amount").isNull() | F.col("txn_timestamp").isNull())

print(f"Valid Silver Records: {df_valid.count()}")
df_valid.show(truncate=False)

df_quarantine.show(truncate=False)

    ("LEAD-1", "  JOHN.DOE@GMAIL.COM  ", "Phone: (555) 123-4567 | City: New York, NY"),
    ("LEAD-2", "SARAH_CONNOR@skyNET.io", "Cell: 555.987.6543 | City: Los Angeles, CA"),
    ("LEAD-3", "unknown_user", "No contact provided | City: Chicago, IL"),
    ("LEAD-4", "bruce.wayne@WayneEnt.com ", "Direct: +1-555-444-3333 | City: Gotham, NJ")
]

# 2. Extract 10-digit phone number pattern
# Matches (xxx) xxx-xxxx, xxx.xxx.xxxx, or xxx-xxx-xxxx
phone_regex = r"(\d{3})[^\d]?(\d{3})[^\d]?(\d{4})"

df_extracted = df_clean_email.withColumn(
    "phone_digits",
    F.regexp_replace(
        F.regexp_extract(F.col("raw_contact_str"), phone_regex, 0),
        r"[^\d]",
        ""
    )
).withColumn(
    "city",
    F.regexp_extract(F.col("raw_contact_str"), r"City:\s*([A-Za-z\s]+),", 1)
).withColumn(
    "state",
    F.regexp_extract(F.col("raw_contact_str"), r",\s*([A-Z]{2})", 1)
)

df_extracted.select("lead_id", "clean_email", "phone_digits", "city", "state").show(truncate=False)

# --- Execution Step ---
# Mask email username: j***e@domain.com
df_masked = df_extracted.withColumn(
    "masked_email",
    F.regexp_replace(F.col("clean_email"), r"(^.).*(@.*$)", "$1***$2")
).withColumn(
    "masked_phone",
    F.when(
        F.length(F.col("phone_digits")) == 10,
        F.concat(F.lit("***-***-"), F.substring(F.col("phone_digits"), 7, 4))
    ).otherwise(F.lit("UNAVAILABLE"))
)

df_masked.select("lead_id", "masked_email", "masked_phone", "city", "state").show(truncate=False)

]

)

df_duration = df_parsed.withColumn(
    "duration_seconds",
    F.col("dropoff_ts").cast(T.LongType()) - F.col("pickup_ts").cast(T.LongType())
).withColumn(

clinical_data = [
    ("P-01", "Metabolic", 98.6, 120.0, "NORMAL"),
    ("P-02", "Cardiac", float("nan"), 145.0, "ELEVATED"),
    ("P-03", "Metabolic", None, None, None),
    ("P-04", "Cardiac", 101.2, float("nan"), "CRITICAL"),
    ("P-05", "Metabolic", 97.9, 115.0, "NORMAL"),
    ("P-06", "Neurology", None, 130.0, None)
]

schema = "patient_id STRING, dept STRING, body_temp DOUBLE, systolic_bp DOUBLE, assessment STRING"
df_clinical = spark.createDataFrame(clinical_data, schema)
df_clinical.show()

# --- Execution Step ---
# Build expressions dynamically for all columns
null_audit_exprs = [
    F.count(
        F.when(F.col(c).isNull() | (F.isnan(F.col(c)) if t in ["double", "float"] else F.lit(False)), c)
    ).alias(f"{c}_missing_count")
    for c, t in df_clinical.dtypes
]

df_audit = df_clinical.agg(*null_audit_exprs)
df_audit.show(truncate=False)

# --- Execution Step ---
# 1. Drop rows with at least 3 null fields
df_filtered = df_clinical.dropna(thresh=3)

# 2. Compute departmental average systolic_bp for imputation
dept_avgs = df_filtered.groupBy("dept").agg(F.round(F.avg("systolic_bp"), 1).alias("avg_bp"))

# 3. Join and coalesce missing readings
df_imputed = df_filtered.join(dept_avgs, on="dept", how="left").withColumn(
    "systolic_bp_imputed",
    F.coalesce(
        F.when(F.isnan(F.col("systolic_bp")), None).otherwise(F.col("systolic_bp")),
        F.col("avg_bp"),
        F.lit(120.0) # default fallback
    )
).withColumn(
    "assessment_clean",
    F.coalesce(F.col("assessment"), F.lit("PENDING_REVIEW"))
)

df_imputed.select("patient_id", "dept", "systolic_bp", "systolic_bp_imputed", "assessment_clean").show()

description: Implement deduplication: (1) `distinct()` for exact row matches, (2) `dropDuplicates([subset])` for primary key deduplication with arbitrary winner selection, and (3) Deterministic deduplication using `row_number()` over Window partitions to retain the latest timestamp record.

webhook_events = [

    ("ORD-102", "CANCELLED","2023-11-20 09:12:00", 85.50),
    ("ORD-103", "CREATED", "2023-11-20 09:15:00", 430.00)
]

# --- Execution Step ---

print(f"Original: {df_webhooks.count()} | After distinct: {df_distinct.count()}")

# dropDuplicates on order_id keeps an arbitrary update
df_arbitrary = df_webhooks.dropDuplicates(["order_id"])
print("Arbitrary dropDuplicates (non-deterministic latest status):")
df_arbitrary.show()

# --- Execution Step ---
window_spec = Window.partitionBy("order_id").orderBy(F.col("updated_at").desc())

df_deterministic = (
    df_webhooks
    .withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(window_spec))
    .filter(F.col("rn") == 1)
    .drop("rn")
)

print("Deterministic Deduplication (Always Keeps Latest Status):")
df_deterministic.orderBy("order_id").show()
notes: `dropDuplicates()` uses a HashAggregate under the hood. While efficient, it is non-deterministic regarding which non-key column values survive if not pre-sorted. Window functions (`row_number`) provide 100% deterministic deduplication by explicitly controlling sorting criteria.

title: #010 Transformations vs Actions, Lazy Evaluation & Lineage Graph
description: Demonstrate Spark's lazy evaluation mechanism. Differentiate between Narrow dependencies (map, filter) and Wide dependencies (groupBy, join, distinct). Inspect the RDD execution lineage graph using `toDebugString()` and profile action execution times.
code:
import os
import sys

        .master("local[*]")
        .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "4")
        .config("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true")
        .config("spark.sql.extensions", "io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension")
        .config("spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog", "org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog")
        .getOrCreate()
    )

from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql import types as T
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("WARN")
print(f"Spark Version: {spark.version}")
print(f"Session Active: {spark.sparkContext.appName}")

# --- Execution Step ---
# Generate sequence of 100,000 numbers
df_nums = spark.range(1, 100001, 1, 4)

# Narrow transformation: filter (stays within partition)
df_narrow = df_nums.filter(F.col("id") % 2 == 0).withColumn("squared", F.col("id") * F.col("id"))

# Wide transformation: groupBy and agg (triggers shuffle across partitions)
df_wide = df_narrow.groupBy(F.col("id") % 10).agg(F.sum("squared").alias("sum_squares"))

print("Transformations registered in Catalyst. No execution has occurred yet!")

# --- Execution Step ---
print("=== RDD LINEAGE GRAPH (toDebugString) ===")
print(df_wide.rdd.toDebugString().decode("utf-8"))

# --- Execution Step ---
import time

start = time.time()
result_count = df_wide.count()
elapsed = time.time() - start

print(f"Action triggered! Result rows: {result_count} (Execution Time: {elapsed:.3f}s)")
df_wide.show()
notes: Spark constructs a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of stages separated by shuffle boundaries. Narrow transformations execute entirely within the same partition in memory (pipelining). Wide transformations require data shuffling across the network to new executor partitions, creating new stages.
use_case: A performance engineering lead must diagnose why a data pipeline fails after running for 40 minutes, only to crash on a lightweight `.count()` action. The team must learn to trace lineage graphs and identify narrow vs wide transformations.

description: Implement the calculation using: (1) Standard Python UDF (`@udf`), (2) Native Spark SQL built-in expressions, and (3) Vectorized Pandas UDF (`@pandas_udf`). Compare execution time, serialization behavior, and memory footprint.

from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql import types as T
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("WARN")
print(f"Spark Version: {spark.version}")
print(f"Session Active: {spark.sparkContext.appName}")

# --- Execution Step ---
df_accounts = spark.range(1, 50001, 1, 4).select(
    F.col("id").alias("account_id"),
    (F.rand(seed=42) * 800 + 300).alias("credit_score"),
    (F.rand(seed=101) * 50000 + 1000).alias("debt_amount"),
    (F.rand(seed=202) * 100000 + 20000).alias("annual_income")
)

df_accounts.show(5)

# --- Execution Step ---
@F.udf(returnType=T.DoubleType())
def calculate_risk_standard(credit_score, debt, income):
    if income == 0 or credit_score is None:
        return 0.0
    dti = debt / income
    score_factor = (850 - credit_score) / 550.0
    return round((dti * 0.6) + (score_factor * 0.4), 4)

import time
t0 = time.time()
df_res1 = df_accounts.withColumn("risk_std", calculate_risk_standard("credit_score", "debt_amount", "annual_income"))
c1 = df_res1.filter(F.col("risk_std") > 0.5).count()
t1 = time.time() - t0
print(f"Standard UDF Count: {c1} in {t1:.3f} seconds")

# --- Execution Step ---
import pandas as pd

@F.pandas_udf(T.DoubleType())
def calculate_risk_vectorized(credit_score: pd.Series, debt: pd.Series, income: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    dti = debt / income.replace(0, 1.0)
    score_factor = (850.0 - credit_score) / 550.0
    return ((dti * 0.6) + (score_factor * 0.4)).round(4)

t0 = time.time()
df_res2 = df_accounts.withColumn("risk_vec", calculate_risk_vectorized("credit_score", "debt_amount", "annual_income"))
c2 = df_res2.filter(F.col("risk_vec") > 0.5).count()
t2 = time.time() - t0
print(f"Vectorized Pandas UDF Count: {c2} in {t2:.3f} seconds (Speedup factor: {t1/max(t2, 0.001):.1f}x)")
notes: Standard Python UDFs serialize JVM row data to a Python worker process row-by-row via Py4J, incurring massive serialization and deserialization overhead and disabling Catalyst optimizations. Vectorized Pandas UDFs use Apache Arrow to transfer columnar batches into Pandas Series, achieving near-native C-speed vectorization.
use_case: A credit scoring model applies complex non-linear mathematical risk adjustments to customer accounts. The current implementation uses standard Python UDFs and causes severe CPU throttling and worker memory spikes.

title: #012 Emulating Databricks DBUtils, Widgets & Secret Scopes Locally
description: Design a clean, modular Python compatibility wrapper class `MockDBUtils` that provides identical interfaces for `dbutils.fs` (`ls`, `cp`, `mv`, `rm`, `head`, `put`), `dbutils.widgets` (`text`, `dropdown`, `get`), and `dbutils.secrets` (`get`) using environment variables and local disk storage.
code:
import os
import sys
import shutil
from pathlib import Path

# In Databricks, the SparkSession 'spark' is pre-initialized by the cluster.
# For local PySpark / CI execution, initialize a local session with Delta Lake support:
try:
    spark
except NameError:
    from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
    spark = (
        SparkSession.builder
        .appName("UseCase_012_Emulating_Databricks_DBUtils_Widgets_and_Secret_Scopes_Locally")
        .master("local[*]")
        .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "4")
        .config("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true")
        .config("spark.sql.extensions", "io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension")
        .config("spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog", "org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog")
        .getOrCreate()
    )

from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql import types as T
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("WARN")
print(f"Spark Version: {spark.version}")
print(f"Session Active: {spark.sparkContext.appName}")

# --- Execution Step ---
import os
import shutil
from pathlib import Path

class MockFS:
    def ls(self, path: str):
        p = Path(path.replace("dbfs:", "").replace("file:", ""))
        if not p.exists():
            return []
        class FileInfo:
            def __init__(self, path, name, size):
                self.path = str(path)
                self.name = name
                self.size = size
        return [FileInfo(f, f.name, f.stat().st_size) for f in p.iterdir()]

    def put(self, path: str, content: str, overwrite: bool = True):
        p = Path(path.replace("dbfs:", ""))
        p.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        with open(p, "w") as f:
            f.write(content)

    def head(self, path: str, max_bytes: int = 1000):
        p = Path(path.replace("dbfs:", ""))
        with open(p, "r") as f:
            return f.read(max_bytes)

    def rm(self, path: str, recurse: bool = False):
        p = Path(path.replace("dbfs:", ""))
        if p.is_dir():
            shutil.rmtree(p)
        elif p.exists():
            p.unlink()

class MockWidgets:
    def __init__(self):
        self._widgets = {}

    def text(self, name: str, defaultValue: str, label: str = ""):
        self._widgets[name] = defaultValue

    def dropdown(self, name: str, defaultValue: str, choices: list, label: str = ""):
        self._widgets[name] = defaultValue

    def get(self, name: str):
        return self._widgets.get(name, "")

class MockSecrets:
    def get(self, scope: str, key: str):
        # Resolve from environment variables (e.g. SCOPE_KEY)
        env_key = f"{scope.upper()}_{key.upper()}"
        return os.environ.get(env_key, f"mock-secret-for-{key}")

class DBUtilsEmulator:
    def __init__(self):
        self.fs = MockFS()
        self.widgets = MockWidgets()
        self.secrets = MockSecrets()

# Instantiate emulator
dbutils = DBUtilsEmulator()
print("Universal DBUtils Emulator initialized successfully!")

# --- Execution Step ---
# 1. Put file in mock DBFS
dbutils.fs.put("/tmp/dbfs_test/config.json", '{"environment": "staging", "batch_size": 5000}')

# 2. Read file back with head
content = dbutils.fs.head("/tmp/dbfs_test/config.json")
print("Read Content:", content)

# 3. List directory
files = dbutils.fs.ls("/tmp/dbfs_test")
for f in files:
    print(f"File found: {f.name} ({f.size} bytes)")

# 4. Clean up
dbutils.fs.rm("/tmp/dbfs_test", recurse=True)

# --- Execution Step ---
# Configure notebook widgets
dbutils.widgets.dropdown("env", "staging", ["dev", "staging", "prod"], "Target Environment")
dbutils.widgets.text("processing_date", "2023-11-20", "Batch Date")

current_env = dbutils.widgets.get("env")
proc_date = dbutils.widgets.get("processing_date")
api_key = dbutils.secrets.get(scope="finance_scope", key="stripe_token")

print(f"Running pipeline for ENV={current_env}, DATE={proc_date}")
print(f"Retrieved Secret: {api_key[:4]}**** (Masked)")
notes: In Databricks, `dbutils` is a Java/Scala bridge injected into the Python REPL. Writing pipeline code that imports or references `dbutils` directly creates tight vendor lock-in. Wrapping it in a helper or using Databricks Connect decouples code for multi-cloud and local portability.
use_case: An enterprise migration team develops Databricks pipelines locally inside VS Code or CI/CD test runners before deploying to production workspaces. Code relying on `dbutils.fs`, `dbutils.secrets`, and `dbutils.widgets` crashes outside of Databricks.

user_media = [
    ("U-101", ["Sci-Fi", "Action", "Thriller"], ["HD", "Dolby Atmos", "4K"]),
    ("U-102", ["Romance", "Comedy"], ["SD"]),
    ("U-103", ["Documentary"], ["HD", "Subtitles"]),

]

df_users = spark.createDataFrame(user_media, schema)
